title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Dimensionality Reduction and Feature Extraction · Subject: Unsupervised and Self-Supervised Learning. Seven original questions, four teaching-oriented choices each, seven custom diagrams, and beginner-first explanations.
hero:
PCA · VISUAL OVERVIEW

Many measurements. Fewer directions. Most of the variation.

Learn why PCA creates new features instead of just deleting columns, then follow the mathematics, code, and practical limits.

questions.stem: What is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in Machine Learning, and how does it reduce the number of features in a dataset while preserving as much important information as possible?
options: PCA is a feature-selection method that keeps original columns with the strongest relationship to a known target. This can shorten a dataset, but it depends on labels and does not learn new directions from combinations of its features.

PCA is an unsupervised linear method that combines numeric features into fewer new features called principal components. It keeps the directions showing most variation, so a shorter dataset preserves much of the information without keeping all the original columns.

PCA is a grouping method that assigns each row to a cluster and replaces its measurements with the group label. This can organize similar examples, but it reduces rows to categories rather than creating new feature directions.

PCA is a scaling method that adjusts every original measurement to a common numeric range before training. This can prevent units like meters and centimeters from dominating, but it leaves the same columns and does not produce new coordinates describing shared patterns.
questions.explanation: In simple words: PCA turns many related measurements into fewer new numeric features, keeping the directions where the data varies most.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: PCA stands for Principal Component Analysis. It is an unsupervised, linear method that builds new features called principal components from weighted combinations of the original numeric features. The first components capture the largest share of variance, meaning the strongest patterns of spread in the data. Keeping only those components reduces dimensions while losing as little variance as possible for that number of linear components. Imagine monitoring wearable devices with many correlated sensor readings: PCA can summarize shared movement patterns into a few new measurements. Variance is useful information, but not necessarily the information needed for every task.

questions.stem: Imagine a dataset containing 100 features about thousands of houses, including size, number of rooms, and property measurements. How can PCA combine related information into fewer new features without simply deleting the original features?
options: For these houses, PCA learns weighted combinations of related measurements such as floor area, rooms, and dimensions, then gives each home a few component scores. Each score mixes information from several original columns rather than simply selecting or deleting columns.

For these houses, PCA picks the columns entered most often, such as size, rooms, and age, and keeps only those original measurements. That makes the table shorter, but it never learns new features from the relationships between different measurements.

For these houses, PCA predicts the sale price from labeled examples and uses that prediction as the single new input feature. The result comes from supervised price estimation rather than new axes that preserve variation in unlabeled measurements.

For these houses, PCA groups properties by neighborhood and uses a unique neighborhood identifier code as a feature for each home. That might help regional price reports, but it does not learn how rooms, floor area, and dimensions vary together across different properties.
questions.explanation: In simple words: PCA mixes related house measurements into new scores, such as an overall size pattern, instead of simply dropping columns.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Picture 100 measurements for each of thousands of houses. Floor area, number of rooms, and building dimensions may rise together. PCA can learn a principal component that combines them with learned weights into one size-related score. Another component might summarize other independent patterns in the property measurements. Every house receives a score for each chosen component, so a table with 100 original columns can become a table with a few new columns. Those new columns are not selected originals; they are combinations. Standardize first when the original units need comparable influence.

questions.stem: What are Principal Components in PCA, and how do the first, second, and subsequent components capture different directions of variation in the data?
options: Principal components are the original feature columns sorted from the smallest to the largest spread. The first holds the least variation, while later components repeat its direction to keep the same information visible in multiple columns.

Principal components are the variables most strongly linked to an output label, ranked by prediction accuracy. They can point in similar directions because a supervised model may reuse predictive information instead of seeking perpendicular directions through features.

Principal components are clusters of similar rows, with the first containing the largest cluster and later ones containing smaller groups. They describe membership in groups rather than new perpendicular directions along which measurements vary.

Principal components are new axes formed from combinations of the original numeric features. The first follows the greatest variance; the second captures the most remaining variance at right angles, and later components continue along mutually perpendicular directions.
questions.explanation: In simple words: PC1 points along the biggest spread, PC2 captures the next biggest perpendicular spread, and later components capture smaller remaining patterns.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: A principal component is a direction in feature space, not a cluster or an original column. Imagine measuring delivery trips by distance, travel time, and fuel used. The first component might represent their strongest shared direction of variation. The second finds the largest remaining spread in a direction perpendicular to the first. Every later component is perpendicular to those before it and captures no more variance than the preceding component. They are ranked by explained variance, and a data point becomes a set of scores by projection onto these directions.
questions.figure:
03 / PC1, PC2, PC3

Each new axis captures a different spread

PC1 explains the most variance; PC2 is perpendicular and explains the most remaining variance; subsequent directions continue this pattern.

questions.stem: How does PCA work step by step, including feature centering, standardization when needed, covariance matrices, eigenvectors, eigenvalues, and projecting data onto principal components?
options: PCA first predicts a target for every row, then uses prediction errors to choose the columns most related to the labels. The covariance matrix measures predicted classes, eigenvalues measure classification success, and the dataset keeps selected original columns for later training.

PCA first assigns each row to a cluster, then standardizes the cluster labels and counts how many points fall into each group. Eigenvectors become class names, and the new coordinates are the distances from each example to its assigned cluster center.

PCA centers each numeric feature and standardizes it when comparable scales are needed. It measures shared variation with a covariance matrix, finds eigenvectors as principal directions and eigenvalues as their variances, then projects centered rows onto the chosen directions.

PCA starts by rescaling the target label, compares each original feature with that label, and keeps the largest correlation as its first component. The remaining steps adjust the labels, rather than computing new directions and projecting centered observations onto them.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Center the measurements, scale if needed, find the main variation directions, and project each row onto those directions.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: First subtract each feature's mean to center the dataset. When units differ and each measurement deserves comparable weight, standardize using training-data statistics. Next compute the covariance matrix, which describes how centered features vary together. Its eigenvectors provide candidate principal axes; its eigenvalues tell how much variance each explains. Sort by decreasing eigenvalue, choose the first k axes, and multiply the centered data by those axes to obtain k component scores per row. A factory comparing vibration sensors could use this workflow to summarize correlated signals. In practice, numerical software often uses SVD instead of explicitly constructing covariance.

04 / THE PCA ALGORITHM

questions.stem: How can PCA be implemented using Python and Scikit-learn, and how can explained variance ratios and cumulative explained variance help determine the appropriate number of principal components?
options: In Python, StandardScaler chooses the number of principal components by comparing predicted class labels, while PCA renames existing columns. Explained variance ratios then show model accuracy for each class, and the cumulative curve adds prediction errors instead of feature variation.

In Python, scale numeric features when needed, fit Scikit-learn PCA, and transform rows into component scores. The explained_variance_ratio_ values show each component's share of variance; their cumulative sum helps choose the smallest number reaching a chosen retention threshold.

In Python, PCA fills missing values by ranking feature means, and its largest eigenvalue becomes a prediction score. Cumulative explained variance is calculated from the sum of all original feature averages, so it does not describe the information kept.

In Python, fit a separate PCA model to every test row, allowing each example to have new axes. Then use target accuracy to choose the number of original columns, rather than checking how much of the total feature variation is retained.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Fit PCA in Scikit-learn, read each component's variance share, and add those shares to find how many components retain enough.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Scikit-learn provides PCA in sklearn.decomposition and exposes explained_variance_ratio_ after fit. For the Iris flower dataset, standardizing four numeric measurements gives roughly 73%, 23%, 4%, and 1% of variance across the four components. Together, the first two retain about 96%, so a 95% threshold chooses two components. The cumulative sum reveals this decision clearly. Use a Pipeline with StandardScaler and PCA on the training set to avoid data leakage; transform validation or test data with that fitted pipeline. The included example shows the real Python API and a variance chart.
questions.figure:
05 / PYTHON + VARIANCE

Use explained variance to choose the number of components

Show executable Scikit-learn code and output
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
import numpy as np

X = load_iris().data
full = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA()).fit(X)
ratios = full.named_steps["pca"].explained_variance_ratio_
print(np.round(ratios, 4))          # [0.7296 0.2285 0.0367 0.0052]
print(np.round(np.cumsum(ratios), 4))

reduced = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=0.95, svd_solver="full")
)
scores = reduced.fit_transform(X)
print(scores.shape)                  # (150, 2)

# In a real predictive workflow, fit on TRAIN data only.

Values are calculated from StandardScaler + PCA on the classic Iris dataset. First two PCs explain approximately 95.81% of standardized feature variance.

questions.stem: What is the mathematical relationship between PCA, eigendecomposition, Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and low-rank matrix approximation, and why is SVD often preferred for computing PCA on large datasets?
options: PCA eigendecomposes the covariance matrix; SVD factors centered X as UΣVᵀ. V gives principal axes, and squared singular values divided by n−1 give covariance eigenvalues. Keeping the leading k factors yields the best rank-k least-squares approximation; SVD often improves stability by avoiding explicit covariance.

PCA eigendecomposes a target-label matrix, while SVD finds unrelated directions that mainly represent which features have high means. Keeping the first k original columns gives the best low-rank approximation, and SVD is preferred because it skips the need to center observations.

PCA and SVD give different feature directions because the right singular vectors are unrelated to covariance eigenvectors. A low-rank model keeps the first k training rows instead of dominant patterns, while SVD mainly improves performance by converting numeric features into categorical groups.

PCA finds eigenvectors of the pairwise distance matrix, whereas SVD factors the covariance matrix into cluster labels and numerical weights. Low-rank approximation preserves every original dimension without any loss, and SVD is faster chiefly because its singular values do not require matrix calculations across the dataset.
questions.explanation: In simple words: SVD finds PCA's main directions directly from centered data, and keeping the strongest directions gives a compact best-fit approximation.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Center the data matrix X, then compute SVD: X = UΣVᵀ. The columns of V are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix XᵀX/(n−1), and covariance eigenvalues are squared singular values divided by n−1. Retaining the leading k singular values and vectors gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm; add the feature means back for reconstruction. Imagine compressing a satellite image into its strongest patterns. SVD often avoids explicitly forming covariance, which can improve numerical stability. Full SVD can still be expensive; truncated or randomized SVD may help for large matrices.
questions.figure:
06 / LINEAR ALGEBRA

SVD and eigenvectors describe the same principal axes

The colored matrices show shape and relationships, not numerical values. Rank-k truncated SVD gives the best least-squares low-rank fit to centered data.

questions.stem: What are the limitations of PCA when working with nonlinear relationships, outliers, differently scaled features, and high-dimensional datasets, and when should techniques such as Kernel PCA, Incremental PCA, or other dimensionality reduction methods be considered?
options: PCA normally captures curved relationships and extreme outliers without preprocessing because its directions adjust to every local shape. Kernel PCA is needed only when labels are present, while Incremental PCA is mainly for improving classification results on small, fully loaded tables in practice today.

PCA automatically makes meters and millimeters equally important, and its memory use stays fixed no matter how many rows arrive. Kernel PCA replaces linear PCA in every situation, while Incremental PCA requires loading the entire dataset into memory before it can begin.

PCA cannot work on any numeric measurements until they are turned into categories, but it naturally ignores very distant observations. Dimensionality reduction also preserves every original detail, so nonlinear methods are helpful only when training labels are available for every row.

PCA is linear, so it may miss curved relationships; outliers can rotate its axes, large-scale features can dominate, and large matrices cost memory. Scale and inspect data, use Kernel PCA for nonlinear structure, Incremental PCA for batches, or task-specific alternatives.
questions.explanation: In simple words: PCA can miss curved patterns or be distorted by outliers and units; choose scaling, Kernel PCA, or batch-based methods as needed.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: PCA finds straight, variance-maximizing directions, so a curved shape can remain tangled when flattened. A single extreme outlier can change those directions, and features measured in large units can dominate unless suitable scaling is applied. Very wide or large datasets may strain computation or memory. Consider Kernel PCA for certain nonlinear patterns, IncrementalPCA when data arrives in manageable batches, or robust preprocessing when outliers matter. Methods such as UMAP can support nonlinear visualization, but they have different objectives and may not preserve PCA-style reconstruction. Choose based on the downstream task and validate results.
questions.figure:
07 / WHEN PCA STRUGGLES

Curves, outliers, scale and data size all matter

Consider Kernel PCA for selected nonlinear structures, scaling/robust preparation for distorted features, or IncrementalPCA when data is too large for one fit.
